paperTitle: Singapore-Cambridge GCE O-Level 1184 English Language — AI-authored Simplified Practice 39: The Paper Lantern (§B style, simplified band)
provenanceNote: NOT STUDENT-FACING. AI-authored original narrative for O-Level 1184 §B style practice, simplified-band difficulty; not from a past examination paper. Modelled on the Singapore-Cambridge 1184/02 (formerly 1128) Section B format and calibrated to the SEAB assessment objectives (literal / inferential comprehension, vocabulary in context, language for effect), pitched at students stretching from middle secondary toward the full O-Level standard. Structure: 7 short-answer questions (Q1-Q7 = 11 marks, mixing [1] and [2]) plus a 4-blank emotion flowchart (Q8 = 4 marks) split into independent MCQs so each sub-part can be auto-graded. Total 15 marks.

sections.instruction: Read the narrative text below and answer the questions that follow. Section B, Part 1 [11 marks]. Answer in your own words as far as possible.
sections.passage:
Paragraph 1
Every year at the Mid-Autumn Festival the corridors of our block were hung with lanterns, and every year I carried a cheap plastic one that played a tinny song. That year was different. My father had bought me a red paper carp from the market in Chinatown, with black paper fins and a real candle inside, and I had kept it on top of my cupboard all week, waiting for the night of the lantern walk.

Paragraph 2
At seven o'clock the children of the estate gathered at the void deck. My father lit my candle for me and then went back up to our flat to watch from the corridor, and the carp glowed from the inside like something alive. We paraded along the path between the blocks, a slow line of small lights, and I walked near the front with both hands around the handle, holding it as steadily as I could.

Paragraph 3
I do not know whether it was the wind or my own arm that did it. The handle tipped, the lantern swung, and the flame touched the paper side.

Paragraph 4
The fire ran up the carp faster than I could think. There was a bright curl of flame, a smell of burning paper, and then my beautiful red fish was a curl of grey ash on the ground. I was left holding a bare, charred wire frame. My eyes filled and I could not trust my voice. Ahead of me the line of lanterns moved on without stopping, and I stood at the edge of the path with a handle and nothing else.

Paragraph 5
Then Mei, a girl from the next block, turned back. She looked at the frame in my hand, and at my face, and she did not say anything about the fire at all. She simply held out her white rabbit lantern by the stick and said, 'You hold it first. I'll take it back at the playground.'

Paragraph 6
So the two of us walked the rest of the way with one lantern between us, passing the stick back and forth at every lamp post. Mei made the rabbit hop along the ground and I laughed until my sides hurt, and by the time we reached the playground I had stopped thinking about the ash on the path behind us.

Paragraph 7
That was eight years ago. I could not tell you now what happened to the wire frame, or where the plastic lanterns of the other years went. What I remember, every Mid-Autumn, is not the lantern I lost, but the hand that held one out to me on a dark path.

(Mid-Autumn Festival: a Chinese festival held in autumn, when children carry lanterns after dark. carp: a large freshwater fish, a common shape for Chinese paper lanterns. void deck: the open ground floor of a Singapore HDB block, used for community gatherings.)

questions.stem: Q1. From Paragraph 1, what was the narrator's new lantern made of, and what shape was it? [1]
questions.answer: a red paper carp / a paper lantern in the shape of a fish. Accept any answer giving BOTH the material (paper) and the shape (carp / fish). One mark.

questions.stem: Q2. What does the word 'paraded' in 'We paraded along the path between the blocks' (Paragraph 2) suggest about how the children walked? [1]
questions.answer: Required element: the idea of walking on show / in a procession, displaying the lanterns for others to see. Do NOT award for 'walked slowly in a line' alone — that is lifted from the following clause and does not gloss 'paraded'.

questions.stem: Q3. From Paragraph 6, how did the two girls manage with only one lantern between them? [1]
questions.answer: they took turns / passed the stick back and forth (at every lamp post)

questions.stem: Q4. The narrator says 'My eyes filled and I could not trust my voice.' Using your own words, give TWO reasons why the narrator was so upset at this moment. (Paragraph 4) [2]
questions.answer: MP1 (what was lost): the special lantern the narrator had waited for all week had been destroyed, leaving only a bare, burnt frame; MP2 (being left behind): the other children's lanterns moved on without stopping, so the narrator was left standing alone at the edge of the path with nothing to walk with. Award one mark per distinct point. Do NOT credit 'the smoke / burning paper made the eyes water' — the question asks why the narrator was upset.

questions.stem: Q5. Using your own words, explain why Mei said nothing at all about the fire when she turned back. (Paragraph 5) [2]
questions.answer: MP1 (she could already see it): 'She looked at the frame in my hand, and at my face' — the burnt frame and the narrator's expression told Mei exactly what had happened, so there was nothing that needed saying; MP2 (kindness / sparing feelings): mentioning the accident would only have drawn attention to it and made the narrator feel worse, so she went straight to doing something helpful instead of talking about it. Award one mark per distinct point.

questions.stem: Q6. Using your own words, explain what the narrator means by remembering 'not the lantern I lost, but the hand that held one out to me on a dark path'. (Paragraph 7) [2]
questions.answer: MP1 (the object matters less): the burnt lantern, and all the other lanterns of childhood, have been forgotten — the narrator cannot even say what became of the frame; MP2 (the kindness lasts): what has stayed for eight years is Mei's act of turning back and sharing, which mattered far more than any possession. Award one mark per distinct point; a single well-formed contrast ('she remembers Mei's kindness, not the lantern') may score both marks.

questions.stem: Q7. What is the effect of describing the burnt lantern as 'a curl of grey ash' (Paragraph 4)? [2]
questions.answer: MP1 (the colour and life drain out): the carp had 'glowed from the inside like something alive' and was bright red, whereas 'grey ash' is dull and colourless, so the image shows all the life and beauty gone out of it; MP2 (scale / totality): a whole lantern reduced to one small scrap on the ground shows the loss is complete, with nothing left to save. Also credit the echo of 'a bright curl of flame' in 'a curl of grey ash', which ties the fire to what it leaves behind. Award one mark per distinct point. Do NOT credit 'it happened quickly' alone — that comes from elsewhere in the sentence, not from this phrase.

sections.instruction: Q8. [4 marks in total] The narrator's main feeling changes as the evening goes on. For each moment below, choose ONE word from the bank that best describes the narrator's dominant feeling there. Some words in the bank are not used, and each word may be used once only. Word bank: annoyed / bored / cheerful / dismayed / excited / grateful / jealous / proud.
sections.passage: Refer to the same 'The Paper Lantern' narrative in Exercise 1 above. Read the part of the narrative named in each question, then choose the single word from the bank that best describes how the narrator feels there.
